bearings.paper_claim: On member-Congress LES (n = 13,671; Tables 7-9, all models with session and topic fixed effects): anger -0.037 (95% CI -0.046 to -0.029, p < 0.001) is the only significant negative emotion term; enthusiasm +0.016 (CI 0.007 to 0.025) and pride +0.011 (CI 0.003 to 0.019, p < 0.01) are positive; fear, disgust, sadness, joy and hope are not significant. Marginal R2 is 0.113 to 0.118 in Tables 7-8 and 0.118 to 0.119 in Table 9. The paper reports no controls-only model, so an incremental R2 for emotion terms is not stated.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.4, Figure 4, Tables 7-9 (text labels read 'Tables 7, 7, and 9')
bearings.system_side: lep_criterion.py loads CEL House and Senate LES 93rd-118th and scores it against the blended score (bar B: rho >= +0.30 convergent). Its docstring says LES rewards majority and chair status. The claim that the five-stage shadow is not activated was not checked (outside the lines read).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfers as context only: speech tone is a small associational correlate of LES once structural controls are in, so a shadow-vs-LES gap should not be read as a rhetoric effect. No identification, so not usable as a predictor. Quote coefficients as UNSTRATIFIED with window 93rd-118th Congresses and n = 13,671 member-Congresses; the paper pools over majority-flip fault lines.
bearings.verifier_note: Coefficients and CIs match Tables 7-8 exactly. Softened: 'adds about 0.005 R2 beyond controls' is the analyst's inference, not reported (no nested model). Marginal R2 values corrected as above. Code claims confirmed at lep_criterion.py docstring lines 2-22 (CEL House plus Senate 93-118, bar B rho >= +0.30, LES rewards majority and chair status).

bearings.paper_claim: Mixed models of speech-level emotion (Tables 5-6; n = 1,766,113 speeches; session and topic fixed effects): senators express less anger (-0.041, CI -0.043 to -0.039) and more pride (+0.009) and joy (+0.008); women express more fear (+0.004) and sadness (+0.006); majority members express less anger (-0.035); ideology score predicts more anger (+0.022). Mann-Kendall trends (Table 3, 26 Congresses): 15 of 16 party-by-emotion series increase significantly; Democratic joy does not (tau 0.243, FDR p 0.086).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.1 and Table 3; Sec 4.3 and Tables 5-6
bearings.system_side: affective_n is the mean of LLM affective facets (pessimism, anxiety, depression, volatility), residualized on E and then on a Republican dummy only; it is not residualized on chamber, gender or ideology. The LIWC-style anchor is a hand-written regex approximation (FPS, NEG, POS patterns), not the LIWC dictionary. The interview-to-floor transfer result (rho .050) was not located in this file.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds only weakly. Within one Congress majority status is nearly collinear with party, so the party residual may cover it. Chamber and gender are not covered and are a plausible structural confound. The paper's coefficients are mostly 0.001 to 0.04 in standardized units. The paper's facets are fear and sadness on floor text, not the interview facets used here.
bearings.verifier_note: Verified: senator anger -0.041, senator pride 0.009 and joy 0.008, women fear 0.004 and sadness 0.006, majority anger -0.035, ideology anger 0.022; code residualization on E and a party dummy confirmed. Refuted sub-claim: 'all eight emotions trend upward in both parties' is wrong, since Democratic joy is not significant (Table 3). Softened: the anchor is a regex approximation of LIWC-style categories, not LIWC itself. The majority-party collinearity point is the analyst's inference.

bearings.paper_claim: In LES models (Table 9): valence (positive minus negative emotion) +0.020 (CI 0.011 to 0.028) and intensity -0.014 (CI -0.025 to -0.004, p < 0.01). The paper reads the rise in emotion since 1973 as intensification with both positive and negative emotions rising, not as a negative turn. In the paper, intensity is the sum of the eight z-scored emotion scores.
bearings.system_side: stage5_lsd.R emits lsd_net (pos minus neg), lsd_net_norm (net divided by words) and lsd_charge ((pos plus neg) divided by words) per text. lsd_charge is a normalized dictionary-count magnitude, not a sum of classifier scores.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports keeping direction and intensity as separate fields rather than collapsing them. Weak transfer: floor speech vs press releases, dictionary vs transformer, and LES outcome vs CU stance or behavior. It does not show whether sign times intensity predicts behavior. Do not treat lsd_charge as the same construct as the paper's intensity; they are analogous only.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers match Table 9 and the Sec 4.1 reading. Softened: 'lsd_charge matches the paper intensity construct' overstates it; the paper's intensity is a sum of classifier z-scores and lsd_charge is a normalized dictionary count. Code confirmed at stage5_lsd.R lines 45-60. Not checked: the component card wording (intensity as |net|/words) since the brain card was not read.

related.why: Cited by this paper for emotion in parliamentary debates. The item uses lexicons (dictionaries), not the transformer classifier used here, so it is an earlier lexicon approach rather than a same-method link.
Cited for emotive rhetoric in parliaments. The item uses a dictionary-based measure. This paper mentions strategic and communicative functions of emotion in its limitations but does not test them.
Not cited by this paper. The item measures emotional intensity of congressional floor speech from vocal pitch, an acoustic counterpart to the text intensity measure here.
Not cited by this paper. The item infers member traits from speech and links them to sponsorship behavior. The same-data label was not confirmed, so the relation was changed to complements.
Not cited by this paper. This paper names subnational legislatures as a future test (Limitations); the item is an LES study of American state legislatures.

Not cited by this paper. The item uses the Volden-Wiseman effectiveness measure, the same outcome this paper uses, and offers a bipartisanship account that an emotion account would need to be separated from.
Not cited by this paper. The item uses sponsorship networks with the Volden-Wiseman effectiveness outcome, a competing non-rhetorical correlate that this paper does not control.
Not cited by this paper. The item builds corpus-based sentiment dictionaries for specialized vocabularies, a dictionary alternative relevant to the LSD-tone vs classifier contrast.

summary_issues: 'The classifier was built on German political text' is inferred from the cited title of Widmann and Wich 2023; the paper does not state the training language. Say the cited source is a German-text study.

'Marginal R2 moves only from about 0.113 to 0.119, so emotion adds little beyond the controls' is not supported: no controls-only model is reported, and the 0.113 to 0.119 range comes from models that all include emotion terms.
'Its valence vs intensity split matches the two LSD fields' is overstated; see bearing 3. Analogous, not the same construct.
'It uses the same CEL LES that lep_criterion.py pulls' is plausible (code reads CEL 93-118) but equivalence to the paper's Volden-Wiseman file was not checked at data level.
'Interview-to-floor genre transfer already FAILED (rho .050)' is not in emit_affective_n.py and was not verified elsewhere.
Effect-size ranges are inconsistent: the summary-level text says 0.001 to 0.02 SD in one place and 0.004 to 0.04 SD in another; Tables 5-6 absolute coefficients run 0.000 to 0.041.
'Paul's recorded position on the effectiveness shadow' (paul_alignment) is unverified: the item has no paul_entries and the brain was not read. Drop it or verify it before use.
Summary's 'nearly every emotion rises in both parties' is correct (15 of 16 series); the one exception, Democratic joy, should be named where the trend claim is repeated.
Summary's note on internal inconsistencies (random intercepts in Sec 3.3 vs fixed-effects table notes; Table 9 text vs column labels) is correct.
